newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia closes deal for $2 billion oil pipeline.
newsitem.headline: Russia closes deal for $2 billion oil pipeline.

text.p: Russia formally closed the biggest foreign investment deal in its history Friday when Energy Minister Boris Nemtsov signed a contract for the construction of a $2 billion oil pipeline.

"This is the biggest investment project in Russian history," Nemtsov said after the signing ceremony with officials of the Caspian Pipeline Consortium, which will build the 940-mile pipeline linking massive oil reserves in western Kazakhstan to Russia's Black Sea oil port of Novorossiisk.
The agreement will allow full financing of the project to proceed and construction to begin, the consortium said.
"The project is of the utmost importance to Russia. It will bring $23 billion to Russia (over 40 years), or more than 10 times the (government's) total outstanding debt to pensioners," Nemstov said.

The Caspian Pipeline Consortium, comprising eight companies and three governments, plans to transport about 560,000 barrels a day through the pipeline in the early stages, building volumes gradually to 1.34 million bpd by 2014.
San Francisco-based Chevron Corp., with a 15 percent stake, is the largest single shareholder among the companies in the consortium.
Jeet Bindra, president of Chevron Pipe Line Co., said he expected the line to be completed by September 1999 and oil to flow shortly thereafter.
But officials added that the consortium still needed to complete feasibility studies, environmental reports and rights of way agreements before it could dig ditches and lay pipes.
"We are aiming at construction starting at the start of 1998," Bindra said.

Attracting foreign investment to Russia's ailing oil industry has proved painfully slow since reforms began in the early 1990s. Friday's ceremony reinforced the impression that personalities still count in getting deals done.

Consortium members said that Nemtsov, who is also First Deputy Prime Minister and a rising star in President Boris Yeltsin's reformist cabinet, played a key role in pushing the deal through a myriad of bureaucratic traps.
"He personally was very instrumental in getting the decrees signed that were necessary," said Richard Matzke, president of Chevron Overseas Petroleum Inc.
Nemtsov in turn handed the praise to his president.
"Only the intervention of Boris Yeltsin allowed this deal to get through the bureacracy," Nemtsov said. "It was only a month ago that today's signing was in grave doubt."
While the project does not involve oil production on Russian soil, Russia is set to earn huge transport fees.
Its largest oil company, LUKoil, has a 12.5 percent stake in the consortium and state oil company Rosneft a 7.5 percent share.
The Russian government also owns 24 percent of the consortium, and may divide its share equally between LUKoil, Rosneft and Transneft, the nation's oil pipeline monopoly.

The Caspian Pipeline Consortium's shareholders also include Mobil Corp. with 7.5 percent, Britain's BG Plc (formerly British Gas) and Italy's Agip SpA with 2 percent each, and Oryx Energy Co. and Munaigaz of Kazakhstan with 1.75 percent each.
The remaining 50 percent is divided among Russia (24 percent), Kazakhstan (19 percent) and Oman (7 percent).
